hero.headline: Rubio testifies to Congress as Iran peace talks stall
hero.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio appeared before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Tuesday, offering his first public testimony since the Trump administration launched military operations against Iran in February. His testimony came as Tehran announced it was halting peace talks with the United States, citing Israeli military operations in Lebanon as a violation of ceasefire agreements.

Despite Iran's announcement to stop exchanging messages with Washington through intermediaries, Rubio expressed optimism about the diplomatic path forward. He told senators that Iran has agreed to negotiate aspects of its nuclear program that it had refused to discuss just a month earlier.

"There is the prospect before us, which could happen today, it could happen tomorrow, it could happen next week that for the first time, certainly in my memory, they have agreed to negotiate aspects of their nuclear program that just a month ago they said they would not," Rubio stated.

The secretary outlined a two-phase framework for potential negotiations. He said reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with Iran committing to remove mines, avoiding tolls, and pledging not to fire on ships, must come first as a precondition for talks rather than a bargaining chip. "That's the predicate that opens the door to phase two," Rubio explained.

Phase two would require Iran to dispose of its highly enriched uranium stockpile and negotiate strict, long-term limitations or cancellation of its enrichment activities. When asked by Senator Chris Murphy whether sanctions relief might be offered simply to reopen the waterway, Rubio rejected that idea, saying any sanctions relief would be tied to Iran's nuclear program.

Rubio also addressed the current blockade affecting Iranian oil revenue. He stated that Washington's counter-blockade, implemented after Iran allegedly failed to honor its commitment to reopen the strait under an April ceasefire agreement, costs Tehran "hundreds of millions of dollars a day" in lost revenue. "If they're going to shut down the straits for everybody, we're going to shut down the straits for them," Rubio said.

On Iran's military capabilities, Rubio claimed the country's missile program had been "substantially degraded" and its launcher capacity reduced. He stated that Iran's drone-building capability has been "eroded," though he acknowledged the regime still possesses numerous drones because they are relatively easy to manufacture.

The New York Times has reported, however, that Iran retained roughly 70 percent of its prewar missile stockpile, though analysts noted that over 85 percent of Iran's ballistic missile, drone, and naval defense industrial base has been damaged or destroyed.

Rubio's testimony reflects growing congressional pressure on the administration to clarify its Iran strategy as regional tensions persist and diplomatic efforts remain at an impasse.

cards.headline: Trump signs executive order giving government early access to AI models
cards.body:
President Trump signed an executive order creating a voluntary framework for federal government review of powerful artificial intelligence models before public release. The order represents a shift from Trump's initial deregulatory approach to AI policy, which included revoking a Biden-era executive order on AI safety standards.

Under the new framework, technology companies are asked to share advanced AI models with the government for voluntary review up to 30 days before releasing them publicly. The Trump administration says this process will strengthen national security and cybersecurity protections. The order stops short of imposing mandatory review requirements, reflecting compromises made after industry objections and internal administration disagreements over how strictly to regulate the sector.

The executive order emerged after weeks of debate within the Trump administration. Some supporters pushed for stricter mandatory review processes, while technology industry advocates argued for lighter regulation to maintain competitive advantage. According to reports, Trump initially planned to back a stricter safety review requirement but reversed course, citing concerns about slowing American AI development and competition with China.

The National Security Agency and Department of Defense will help determine which AI models require government scrutiny. The Treasury Department will assist in identifying vulnerabilities within AI systems. The administration also directed the government to hire additional cybersecurity and AI professionals and strengthen cybersecurity systems at critical infrastructure like hospitals and banks.

The move builds on existing arrangements already in place. The Center for AI Standards and Innovation, part of the Department of Commerce, has similar agreements with OpenAI and Anthropic. The federal government recently made a deal with Microsoft, Google DeepMind, and xAI for early model reviews, though details of that agreement were subsequently removed from the government website.

The framework comes as AI safety experts and governments express growing concern about the capabilities of advanced AI models. Recent developments, including systems with sophisticated cybersecurity abilities, have raised alarms about potential misuse if these tools reach the wrong actors.

The Trump administration frames this approach as necessary for national security while maintaining innovation. However, free speech advocates have raised concerns that excessive government control over AI development could lead to censorship. Trump has also signed another AI-focused executive order aimed at preventing individual states from regulating artificial intelligence, establishing a federal taskforce to challenge state AI laws.

The voluntary nature of the review process means companies maintain the ability to decline participation, distinguishing this approach from stricter regulatory models that other countries have pursued.

cards.headline: Medicaid work requirements finalized by Trump administration
cards.teaser: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services issued a final rule requiring most Medicaid recipients to work or volunteer.
cards.body:
The Trump administration issued a final rule requiring most Medicaid beneficiaries between ages 19 and 64 to document work or community service activities to maintain coverage. This represents a significant change to the Medicaid program's eligibility requirements.

Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, addressed the new requirements at a White House briefing Tuesday afternoon.

cards.headline: Trump names Bill Pulte acting director of national intelligence
cards.teaser: President Trump appointed Bill Pulte to serve as acting director of national intelligence.
cards.body:
President Trump has appointed Bill Pulte, the head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, as acting director of national intelligence. The move comes days after Tulsi Gabbard stepped down from the role.

Pulte, a close Trump ally and heir to a home construction company fortune, will serve in the position without requiring Senate confirmation. As acting director, he will oversee the nation's 18 intelligence agencies and provide national security advice to the president.

cards.headline: Russian strikes kill 22 in Ukraine as Moscow signals weakness on battlefield
cards.body:
Russia launched a devastating overnight assault on Ukraine, firing 73 missiles and 656 drones across multiple cities and killing at least 18 people, according to the air force. The attack targeted Kyiv, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Poltava, and Kharkiv, with eight hypersonic Tsirkon missiles among the weapons deployed.

In Kyiv, six people died and 66 were injured, including three children. A 24-storey apartment block was struck, triggering a partial collapse, while a nine-storey building caught fire. In the Podilskyi district, residents were trapped under rubble as rescue operations continued through the night. Power was cut for 140,000 residents, though utility workers later restored electricity to 110,000 people.

The attack on Dnipro proved particularly deadly, with at least 12 killed and 37 injured. A three-year-old boy was among the dead after a four-storey residential building collapsed. Six people remained missing in the rubble, and a rescuer was killed during a second strike on the same location. The city's mayor accused Russia of deliberately using cluster munitions in residential areas to maximize civilian casualties.

Ukraine's air defenses intercepted about half the missiles fired, but more than 30 struck civilian targets. The assault prompted President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to appeal directly to Donald Trump for Patriot missiles, which he described as a vital tool for protecting against ballistic weapons.

"If Ukraine is not protected from ballistic and other missile strikes, these strikes will continue," Zelenskyy said on social media. "Europe needs its own anti-ballistic missiles so that this war can finally end."

Zelenskyy has repeatedly warned that Ukraine is running out of Patriot interceptors, the only air defense system capable of stopping fast-moving ballistic missiles. He previously wrote to the White House and Congress requesting assistance, calling the weapons crucial for saving lives. The Trump administration has not yet responded to these requests.

Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, characterized the strikes as evidence of Russian desperation. "Putin is a war criminal and loser who has no cards except terror," he said. "Moscow is losing on the battlefield. No number of missiles can change this."

The attack came as Ukraine has waged an increasingly successful aerial campaign with long-range drones, targeting Russian oil refineries, ports, and a key land corridor connecting occupied southern Ukraine with Crimea. Military analysts suggest Russia is attempting to gain leverage through intensified civilian strikes rather than achieving military objectives.

Zelenskyy had warned of the possibility of major strikes on Monday, urging residents to pay close attention to air raid alerts. The overnight bombardment left much of Kyiv scarred with destruction and debris.

cards.headline: Israel continues strikes in southern Lebanon after holding off on Beirut
cards.teaser: Israeli forces attacked southern Lebanon while maintaining a partial truce that spared the capital.
cards.body:
Israel has continued its military campaign in southern Lebanon while avoiding strikes on Beirut following a deal announced by the United States. Under pressure from President Trump, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu chose not to attack the capital, though he pledged to maintain operations against Hezbollah.

A partial truce between Israel and Hezbollah appears to be holding as Israeli forces remain active in the southern region of the country.

cards.headline: S&P 500 Reaches New Record High Led by Nvidia and Chip Stocks
cards.teaser: The S&P 500 climbed to a fresh record high with semiconductor stocks leading gains.
cards.body:
The S&P 500 reached a new record high during trading, with semiconductor stocks leading the advance. Nvidia spearheaded gains in the chip sector, contributing significantly to the broader market rally.

The strong performance reflects investor confidence in technology stocks, particularly those tied to artificial intelligence and advanced computing applications. This latest record extends a period of sustained strength for major US indexes.

cards.headline: Two killed in Kenya protests over US Ebola quarantine center
cards.teaser: Police shot two people dead during demonstrations against a planned American treatment facility.
cards.body:
Two people were shot dead during protests in Kenya against a proposed US Ebola quarantine center. Demonstrations erupted near the planned facility site at Laikipia Air Base in Nanyuki, about 120 miles from Nairobi.

Local residents strongly oppose the US plan to establish the quarantine facility for American citizens with Ebola symptoms. Kenyans fear the center will expose them to the virus in a country with no known cases. Critics argue the US should quarantine its citizens domestically rather than sending them abroad, viewing the proposal as unfair and indicative of double standards.

cards.headline: Israel continues strikes in southern Lebanon after holding off on Beirut
cards.teaser: Israeli forces attacked southern Lebanon while maintaining a partial truce that spared the capital.
cards.body:
Israel has continued its military campaign in southern Lebanon while avoiding strikes on Beirut following a deal announced by the United States. Under pressure from President Trump, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu chose not to attack the capital, though he pledged to maintain operations against Hezbollah.

A partial truce between Israel and Hezbollah appears to be holding as Israeli forces remain active in the southern region of the country.

cards.headline: British couple loses appeal of Iran prison sentences
cards.teaser: Lindsay and Craig Foreman will remain imprisoned after their appeal was rejected.
cards.body:
A British couple imprisoned in Iran lost their appeal against jail sentences, according to family members. Lindsay and Craig Foreman were arrested in January 2025 while traveling through the country during a global motorbike journey.

The couple's family confirmed the appeal was rejected by Iranian authorities. The Foremans had been detained for over a year before the appeal process concluded.

cards.headline: Two Mozambican men killed in South Africa amid anti-migration protests
cards.teaser: Police are investigating the deaths following violent demonstrations in Mossel Bay.
cards.body:
South African police are investigating the deaths of two Mozambican men in the coastal town of Mossel Bay following violent anti-migration protests. The killings mark the first deaths officially linked to the wave of anti-migrant demonstrations sweeping the country.

Mozambique has claimed that five of its citizens were killed in what it describes as "xenophobic attacks" in South Africa over the weekend. The country is working to repatriate hundreds of its nationals from the region as tensions over undocumented migration continue to escalate into violence.

cards.headline: Canada requests renewal of North American trade agreement
cards.teaser: Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc formally asked the US and Mexico to renew the USMCA pact.
cards.body:
Canada has formally requested the renewal of the North American free trade agreement, with Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc communicating the proposal to his US and Mexican counterparts in a letter. LeBlanc indicated that the three countries should move forward with renewing the USMCA trade deal.

The request initiates the process for reviewing the trilateral trade pact that governs commerce between the United States, Canada, and Mexico. The USMCA replaced the previous NAFTA agreement and is subject to periodic review by member nations.

cards.headline: Stephen Curry signs deal with Chinese sneaker company Li-Ning
cards.teaser: The NBA star joined other players partnering with Chinese sportswear brands.
cards.body:
Stephen Curry reached an agreement with Chinese sneaker company Li-Ning that includes plans for sportswear, athleisure products, and retail stores across the United States and China. The deal marks another major NBA player signing with a Chinese brand.

The partnership will expand beyond footwear to include a broader range of athletic apparel and retail locations in both countries. The agreement follows a trend of prominent basketball players forming partnerships with Chinese sportswear manufacturers.

cards.headline: Voters cast ballots in primary elections across multiple states
cards.teaser: Polls opened for primary elections across the United States, with races in Iowa, New Jersey, California, and other states.
cards.body:
Voting is underway across the United States as primary elections take place in multiple states. The busy election day includes various races at the state and local levels, with voters determining which candidates will advance to general elections later this year.

Republicans are competing in several state-level primary contests as they seek to gain ground in key races across the country.

cards.headline: Trump says Iran negotiations continuing despite complexity
cards.teaser: President Trump stated that negotiations with Iran remain ongoing, describing a potential deal as difficult to achieve.
cards.body:
President Trump said negotiations with Iran are continuing, telling reporters that reaching an agreement is not a simple thing. The comments suggest diplomatic efforts between the two countries remain active despite past tensions.

Trump has previously expressed willingness to engage with Iran on nuclear and regional security issues. The complexity he cited reflects longstanding disagreements between Washington and Tehran on multiple fronts.

cards.headline: Two killed during protests in Kenya over US Ebola quarantine center
cards.teaser: Two people were shot dead during protests against a planned US quarantine facility for Ebola patients in Kenya.
cards.body:
Two people were shot dead during protests in Kenya against a US proposal to establish an Ebola quarantine center in the country. The facility would treat American citizens with Ebola symptoms, sparking public anger and demonstrations near the proposed site at Laikipia Air Base in Nanyuki, about 120 miles from Nairobi.

Local residents have strongly opposed the plan, arguing that Kenya should not accept the risk of housing Ebola patients when the country has no known cases. Protesters say sick foreigners should be quarantined in their home countries rather than being brought to Kenya. A Kenyan court extended an order blocking construction of the facility as resistance to the US plan continues to grow.

cards.headline: British couple loses appeal of Iran jail sentence
cards.teaser: A British couple jailed in Iran had their sentence appeal rejected, according to family members.
cards.body:
Lindsay and Craig Foreman lost their appeal against jail sentences in Iran, their family said. The couple was arrested in January 2025 while traveling through Iran on a global motorbike journey.

The rejection of the appeal means the Foremans will continue serving their sentences in Iranian custody. The family disclosed the court decision but provided no timeline for potential future legal options.

cards.headline: Water company fined over parasite outbreak that sickened 140 in Devon
cards.teaser: South West Water received a fine of 1.8 million pounds following a parasite outbreak in Devon.
cards.body:
South West Water has been fined £1.8 million following a parasite outbreak in Devon. The contamination resulted in more than 140 cases of sickness and diarrhoea, with four people requiring hospital treatment.

The fine was issued after an investigation into how the water supply became contaminated. The outbreak affected residents across the county before the source was identified and resolved.

hero.headline: Job Openings Rose to 7.6 Million in April Despite War Impact
hero.body:
UK Housing Market Gains Momentum Despite Middle East Uncertainty

UK house prices have surged unexpectedly in April, marking the fastest annual growth in 11 months even as the economy grapples with disruptions from the Iran conflict. According to Nationwide, the country's largest building society, property prices rose 3% year-over-year in April, up from 2.2% the previous month. The typical UK home is now valued at £278,880.

The monthly figures tell a similar story of resilience. Prices climbed 0.4% in April, defying economists' forecasts of a 0.3% decline. This marks the fourth consecutive month of price increases. When measured over three months to smooth out volatility, the growth rate reached 1.2%, the highest since February 2025.

Robert Gardner, Nationwide's chief economist, acknowledged the surprise: "Despite the uncertainty caused by developments in the Middle East and the subsequent rise in energy prices, the UK housing market has continued to regain momentum following the slowdown recorded around the turn of the year."

The strength of the housing market stands in stark contrast to weakening consumer sentiment. Consumer confidence has deteriorated noticeably, with the GfK confidence barometer falling to its lowest level since October 2023 in April. A separate survey of estate agents revealed that new buyer inquiries and property sales fell sharply in March, with expectations for future sales becoming significantly more pessimistic.

Lenders have also tightened conditions since the Middle East conflict began, withdrawing some mortgage products and increasing rates. The Bank of England held interest rates steady this week but signaled that increases may be necessary if energy costs remain elevated.

Despite these headwinds, Gardner suggested that household finances remain relatively healthy. "The market is likely being supported by the relative strength of household finances," he said. "In aggregate, household debt is at its lowest level relative to income for around two decades, and sizeable savings buffers have been built up in recent years."

However, economists urge caution about the sustainability of these price gains. Rob Wood, chief economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, expressed skepticism about whether the momentum can continue. He suggested that some sales reflected in Nationwide's index may have been agreed during the early stages of the Iran conflict, before the full economic impact became apparent. "Unfortunately, we doubt prices can keep up their recent pace," Wood said.

The housing market data comes as significant new legislation takes effect. The Renters' Rights Act became law, introducing new protections for tenants including bans on no-fault evictions, limits on annual rent increases tied to market rates, and requirements that landlords reasonably consider pet requests.

cards.headline: Blue Origin Sets Aggressive Timeline for Return to Flight After Explosion
cards.teaser: Blue Origin is moving quickly to resume launches following a rocket explosion that damaged its launchpad.
cards.body:
A Blue Origin New Glenn rocket exploded on its launch pad at Cape Canaveral in Florida. CEO Dave Limp stated that damage to the launchpad was less severe than initially feared, and the company plans to launch New Glenn again this year.

NASA official Jared Isaacman indicated the damaged launchpad may not be fully restored until 2028. Following the explosion, the Space Force announced a new launch deal with Blue Origin. The company has not yet disclosed the cause of the blast.

cards.headline: Victoria's Secret Shares Soar 50% on Strong Sales and Raised Outlook
cards.teaser: Victoria's Secret stock jumped dramatically after the company reported strong bra sales and raised its annual forecast.
cards.body:
Victoria's Secret shares surged 50% after the lingerie retailer reported stronger-than-expected sales and raised its outlook for the year. The company said bra sales powered its turnaround, demonstrating renewed momentum for the brand.

Victoria's Secret now expects annual sales to exceed $7 billion, boosting its previous forecast. The results represent a significant shift for the company, which has worked to rebuild its brand and product lineup in recent years after facing declining sales and changing consumer preferences.

cards.headline: Berkshire Hathaway Invests Additional $10 Billion in Alphabet
cards.teaser: Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway deepened its bet on Google parent Alphabet with a major new investment.
cards.body:
Alphabet announced plans to raise up to $80 billion through an equity offering to fund its artificial intelligence infrastructure investments. Berkshire Hathaway purchased $10 billion worth of shares as part of this fundraising round.

The $80 billion raise represents the largest equity fundraising ever recorded, surpassing the combined value of the three largest initial public offerings. The capital infusion underscores the significant financial demands of building out AI capabilities across the tech sector.

cards.headline: Stephen Curry Signs Deal With Chinese Sneaker Company Li-Ning
cards.teaser: The NBA star reached an agreement with Li-Ning that includes plans for stores across the US and China.
cards.body:
Stephen Curry signed a deal with Chinese sneaker company Li-Ning, marking the latest example of an NBA star partnering with a Chinese brand. The agreement includes plans for sportswear and athleisure products beyond just footwear.

The partnership will involve opening stores across both the United States and China. The deal reflects the growing presence of Chinese athletic brands in the US market and their increasing appeal to high-profile American athletes seeking alternatives to traditional Western sportswear companies.

cards.headline: Trump Megadonor Gave $5.5 Million Estate to Kennedy's Anti-Vaccine Group
cards.teaser: A Mellon family heir transferred a 300-acre Connecticut property to Children's Health Defense at no cost.
cards.body:
A major Trump donor from the Mellon family transferred a Connecticut estate worth $5.5 million to Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s anti-vaccine organization Children's Health Defense last year. The transfer involved adjacent properties covering approximately 300 acres.

The donor provided the real estate at no cost to the organization. The gift represents a significant financial boost to Children's Health Defense, which Kennedy has used as a platform to promote vaccine skepticism and challenge public health policies.

hero.headline: Hackers breach Dashlane password manager, steal customer data vaults
hero.body:
Password management company Dashlane has disclosed a security incident in which attackers gained unauthorized access to customer accounts and downloaded encrypted password vaults. According to the company, hackers exploited a vulnerability in its two-factor authentication system by using brute-force methods to bypass the security layer.

Dashlane is among the largest password management services available, with millions of users relying on the platform to securely store login credentials, payment card information, and other sensitive data. The company encrypts customer password vaults, which means the downloaded data remains scrambled without access to a user's master password. Security researchers have cautioned, however, that weaker master passwords could potentially be cracked through extended computational attacks.

The breach marks a notable security incident within the password management sector, an industry that has promoted itself as a more secure alternative to the widespread practice of reusing passwords across multiple online accounts. As cybersecurity threats have multiplied, both businesses and individual users have increasingly adopted password managers to generate and maintain complex, unique passwords for each account they maintain.

Dashlane has not disclosed the number of affected customers or the duration of the unauthorized access before the breach was detected. The company has also not indicated whether it will require users to change their master passwords or what preventive measures it intends to implement to avoid similar incidents in the future.

The incident reflects a broader pattern of significant breaches targeting password management services in recent years. The successful brute-force attack against two-factor authentication raises broader concerns about the security protocols employed by companies that handle sensitive credential information. Experts have long recommended that password manager users employ exceptionally strong master passwords and activate every available security feature to protect their stored vaults.

Two-factor authentication is generally considered one of the most effective security defenses available, but brute-force attacks can potentially overwhelm systems that lack sufficient protections against repeated login attempts. The vulnerability in Dashlane's implementation suggests that the company's rate-limiting or account lockout mechanisms may have been insufficient to prevent attackers from conducting sustained password-guessing campaigns.

The breach has implications for the millions of people who depend on Dashlane to manage their digital identities. Many users store years worth of account credentials in password managers, making the security of these platforms essential to protecting their broader online presence. A compromised master password could potentially give attackers access to numerous accounts across different services.

As investigations continue, cybersecurity professionals are likely to scrutinize how password managers implement two-factor authentication and what additional safeguards might be necessary to protect these sensitive repositories of credential data.

cards.headline: Trump signs revised AI executive order requiring voluntary government reviews
cards.teaser: President Trump signed a narrower executive order on AI oversight after industry pushback against earlier proposals.
cards.body:
President Trump signed an executive order establishing a voluntary framework for federal government review of advanced AI models before public release. Under the new rules, tech companies are asked to submit their most powerful AI systems to the government up to 30 days before launching them publicly.

The Trump administration framed the order as a national security measure, emphasizing cybersecurity concerns. The voluntary approach represents a shift from the president's earlier deregulatory stance and reflects compromises made after technology industry groups objected to stricter mandatory oversight requirements.

cards.headline: Anthropic expands AI security program to critical infrastructure in 15 countries
cards.teaser: Anthropic is scaling its Claude Mythos AI system to 150 organizations protecting infrastructure that could affect 100 million people.
cards.body:
Anthropic is expanding Project Glasswing, its security vulnerability detection program, to 150 organizations across 15 countries. The initiative provides access to its Claude Mythos AI system to help organizations in critical infrastructure sectors—including power grids, water systems, healthcare facilities, and communications networks—identify and fix security vulnerabilities.

The expansion targets infrastructure where cyberattacks could potentially impact 100 million people. By scaling the program globally, Anthropic aims to strengthen defenses in sectors vital to public safety and essential services.

cards.headline: UN warns next El Niño could be strongest in decades
cards.teaser: A new El Niño phase could begin within weeks and boost temperatures on a planet already strained by climate change.
cards.body:
The United Nations has warned that a new El Niño weather pattern could emerge within weeks, potentially becoming the strongest in decades. This natural climate phenomenon, characterized by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, would further elevate global temperatures on a planet already affected by climate change.

El Niño typically occurs every few years and disrupts weather patterns worldwide, often triggering extreme heat, drought, and flooding across different regions.

cards.headline: OpenAI releases new Codex tools for enterprise workplace automation
cards.teaser: OpenAI expanded its Codex AI system with new capabilities designed for white-collar work and knowledge workers.
cards.body:
OpenAI is expanding its focus on enterprise customers by releasing new capabilities for Codex designed for workplace use. The AI lab unveiled tools aimed at automating tasks in white-collar work environments.

The company released an internal report examining how Codex is currently being used for knowledge work. The research informed the development of these new capabilities for professional settings.

cards.headline: Blue Origin sets timeline for return to flight operations
cards.teaser: Blue Origin announced an aggressive schedule to resume launch operations after reviewing its ground infrastructure.
cards.body:
Blue Origin is pursuing an aggressive timeline to resume launches following an explosion of its New Glenn rocket at Cape Canaveral in Florida. CEO Dave Limp reported that damage to the launchpad was less severe than initially feared. The company plans to launch New Glenn again this year.

An inspection of Blue Origin's launch facilities revealed that critical infrastructure remains intact. The propellant farm and storage tanks for oxygen, liquid hydrogen, and liquefied natural gas are all in good condition, supporting the accelerated return-to-flight schedule.

cards.headline: Board, game startup from Mirror founder, raises $20 million
cards.teaser: Board closed a Series A funding round led by Union Square Ventures and has already sold thousands of units.
cards.body:
Board, a game startup founded by Mirror creator Brynn Putnam, has closed a Series A funding round led by Union Square Ventures worth $20 million. The company describes itself as building "together tech" designed to bring people into the same physical space.

The startup has already achieved significant traction, selling thousands of units of its product. This represents Putnam's second venture following Mirror, the home fitness company that Lululemon acquired for $500 million in 2020.

hero.headline: White House Correspondents Association Reschedules Dinner After Assassination Attempt on Trump
hero.body:
The White House Correspondents Association announced plans to reschedule its annual awards dinner for July 24 following a shooting incident at the Washington Hilton that forced an evacuation of President Donald Trump and hundreds of guests.

Weijia Jiang, president of the organization, informed members of the new date in a letter issued Tuesday. The original event was interrupted when a suspect charged a Secret Service checkpoint armed with a shotgun, a handgun, and multiple knives.

According to officials, the suspect was tackled to the ground by Secret Service members and apprehended. A Secret Service agent was injured during the incident and transported to a hospital. The suspect, identified as Cole Tomas Allen, 31, of Torrance, California, was also taken to a hospital for evaluation and faced felony firearm and assault charges.

Interim Metropolitan Police Chief Jeffery Carroll explained that the suspect appeared to have been a lone gunman who was staying at the hotel, which allowed him to pass through the outermost layer of security. The hotel had been closed to the public from 2 p.m. in anticipation of the 8 p.m. dinner, with access restricted to hotel guests, ticket holders, and people with event invitations or White House Correspondents Association credentials.

The roughly 2,300 guests in the ballroom had to pass through multiple security checkpoints, including ticket verification and magnetometer screening. The Secret Service maintained an additional perimeter around the president at the head table, with agents stationed in front of and alongside the stage.

After the shooting, guests hid under tables as Secret Service agents with drawn weapons rushed reporters from the room. Trump later praised law enforcement's response, noting that one officer was saved by wearing a bulletproof vest. Trump said he would have preferred to return and deliver his speech but agreed the gala should be rescheduled within 30 days.

The White House Correspondents Dinner has been a prominent Washington fixture for decades, bringing together journalists, government officials, and celebrities for speeches and journalism awards. The event has occasionally been controversial, with some presidents declining to attend, but security incidents of this magnitude have been rare.

The association's decision to proceed with a rescheduled dinner demonstrates its commitment to maintaining the annual tradition while addressing the serious security concerns raised by the shooting. The July 24 date allows security personnel and event organizers additional time to coordinate enhanced protective measures for what remains one of the most significant annual gatherings of political journalists and government officials in the nation's capital. The announcement reflects efforts to move forward from the alarming incident while prioritizing attendee safety.

cards.headline: Ofcom Calls Married at First Sight UK Allegations Deeply Disturbing
cards.teaser: Britain's media watchdog said allegations against the Channel 4 reality program are being treated seriously.
cards.body:
Ofcom, the UK's broadcasting regulator, has described allegations against Channel 4's Married at First Sight UK as deeply disturbing and says it is taking them very seriously. The reality show, which matches strangers for marriage, is now facing regulatory scrutiny.

Two women have told the BBC they were raped while appearing on the program. Insiders have also spoken to the BBC about an unhealthy focus on sex and a toxic culture surrounding the show's production.

cards.headline: Masters of the Universe Film Draws Mixed Critical Reception
cards.teaser: Critics praised elements of Amazon's He-Man adaptation but identified weaknesses in the big-budget release.
cards.body:
Amazon's Masters of the Universe adaptation, starring Nicholas Galitzine as He-Man, has received mixed reviews on Rotten Tomatoes. The $200 million production draws heavily on the 1980s toy franchise's nostalgia, with some critics praising aspects of the film while others called it a weak misfire in its execution as a superhero adaptation.

The Guardian's review criticized the film as a labored attempt to resurrect toy IP that few people still care about. The film joins a recent trend of studios attempting to revive dormant intellectual property, though major recent successes like Barbie have been based on products with strong ongoing consumer interest.

cards.headline: Katherine LaNasa to Receive Variety Virtuoso Award at Bentonville Film Festival
cards.teaser: The actress will be honored for her career achievements in film and television.
cards.body:
Variety will present Katherine LaNasa with the Variety Virtuoso Award at the Bentonville Film Festival on June 20. The award recognizes her career achievements across film and television, with particular attention to her recent work on the HBO Max series The Pitt.

LaNasa won both an Emmy Award and a Critics Choice Award for Outstanding Supporting performance for her role in The Pitt. The Bentonville Film Festival ceremony will take place on Saturday as part of the festival's programming honoring industry talent.

cards.headline: Russo Brothers Discuss Robert Downey Jr. Costume for Avengers: Doomsday
cards.teaser: The directors said Downey's Doctor Doom costume is their favorite from the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
cards.body:
At SXSW London, directors Anthony and Joe Russo praised Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom costume for Avengers: Doomsday, calling it their favorite from the entire Marvel Cinematic Universe. They highlighted how the design captures the most compelling aspects of the iconic character.

The Russo Brothers appeared on stage for a packed discussion about the upcoming film, scheduled for December release. While they attempted to keep production details under wraps ahead of the film's theatrical debut, they couldn't help but share their enthusiasm for Downey Jr.'s costume design.

cards.headline: Jason Bateman Reflects on Contrasting Roles in Black Rabbit and DTF St. Louis
cards.teaser: The actor discussed playing vastly different characters in two projects released the same year.
cards.body:
Jason Bateman described his experience portraying two widely different characters in the same year, playing a meek weatherman in DTF St. Louis and a man battling substance abuse in Black Rabbit. Bateman said he felt fortunate to take on such contrasting roles in close succession.

The actor also reflected on Netflix's role in reviving Arrested Development, saying the streaming platform saved the comedy series. Bateman has built a career taking on varied roles that showcase different performance styles, from comedy to darker dramatic material.

cards.headline: AMC's The Audacity Cast Discusses Silicon Valley Series at Variety Panel
cards.teaser: Stars of the dark comedy talked about what attracted them to the tech industry-focused show.
cards.body:
Cast members from AMC's The Audacity, including Billy Magnussen and Simon Helberg, appeared at Variety's Behind the Show event to discuss the dark comedy series set in Silicon Valley. Magnussen plays Duncan Park, a data-mining CEO, and said the show's relevance to current technology industry issues drew him to the project.

The panel, presented by AMC, focused on what attracted the actors to the series and its connection to contemporary tech culture. Magnussen described the show as reflecting the industry of the world right now, emphasizing its timely subject matter.

hero.headline: Rubio testifies to Congress as Iran peace talks stall
hero.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio appeared before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Tuesday, offering his first public testimony since the Trump administration launched military operations against Iran in February. His testimony came as Tehran announced it was halting peace talks with the United States, citing Israeli military operations in Lebanon as a violation of ceasefire agreements.

Despite Iran's announcement to stop exchanging messages with Washington through intermediaries, Rubio expressed optimism about the diplomatic path forward. He told senators that Iran has agreed to negotiate aspects of its nuclear program that it had refused to discuss just a month earlier.

"There is the prospect before us, which could happen today, it could happen tomorrow, it could happen next week that for the first time, certainly in my memory, they have agreed to negotiate aspects of their nuclear program that just a month ago they said they would not," Rubio stated.

The secretary outlined a two-phase framework for potential negotiations. He said reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with Iran committing to remove mines, avoiding tolls, and pledging not to fire on ships, must come first as a precondition for talks rather than a bargaining chip. "That's the predicate that opens the door to phase two," Rubio explained.

Phase two would require Iran to dispose of its highly enriched uranium stockpile and negotiate strict, long-term limitations or cancellation of its enrichment activities. When asked by Senator Chris Murphy whether sanctions relief might be offered simply to reopen the waterway, Rubio rejected that idea, saying any sanctions relief would be tied to Iran's nuclear program.

Rubio also addressed the current blockade affecting Iranian oil revenue. He stated that Washington's counter-blockade, implemented after Iran allegedly failed to honor its commitment to reopen the strait under an April ceasefire agreement, costs Tehran "hundreds of millions of dollars a day" in lost revenue. "If they're going to shut down the straits for everybody, we're going to shut down the straits for them," Rubio said.

On Iran's military capabilities, Rubio claimed the country's missile program had been "substantially degraded" and its launcher capacity reduced. He stated that Iran's drone-building capability has been "eroded," though he acknowledged the regime still possesses numerous drones because they are relatively easy to manufacture.

The New York Times has reported, however, that Iran retained roughly 70 percent of its prewar missile stockpile, though analysts noted that over 85 percent of Iran's ballistic missile, drone, and naval defense industrial base has been damaged or destroyed.

Rubio's testimony reflects growing congressional pressure on the administration to clarify its Iran strategy as regional tensions persist and diplomatic efforts remain at an impasse.

cards.headline: Trump appoints Pulte as acting intelligence director
cards.teaser: President Trump named Bill Pulte to lead the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, replacing Tulsi Gabbard.
cards.body:
President Trump has appointed Bill Pulte, the head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, as acting director of national intelligence. Pulte, an heir to a home construction fortune and close Trump ally, takes over the role days after Tulsi Gabbard's resignation.

Democratic lawmakers have strongly criticized the appointment, with some calling Pulte a "partisan thug." The move marks another shift in the administration's national security leadership.

cards.headline: Trump signs executive order on AI and cybersecurity
cards.teaser: The president signed a scaled-back executive order directing agencies to defend against advanced AI threats.
cards.body:
President Trump signed an executive order Tuesday establishing a voluntary framework for federal agencies to review advanced AI models before public release. Under the new rules, tech companies can submit their AI systems to the government for evaluation up to 30 days before launching them publicly.

The order reflects a compromise after industry pushback against earlier versions. The administration aims to address cybersecurity and national security threats posed by AI while avoiding regulations that could slow American technology development.

cards.headline: Judge blocks removal of supercomputer from Colorado climate lab
cards.teaser: A federal judge temporarily halted Trump administration efforts to take a supercomputer from a weather research facility.
cards.body:
A federal judge on Monday blocked the Trump administration from removing a supercomputer from the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Colorado. Judge R. Brooke Jackson issued the preliminary ruling in response to an Office of Management and Budget effort targeting the climate and weather research lab.

The temporary halt prevents the administration from proceeding with the removal while legal proceedings continue. The lab relies on the supercomputer for climate and atmospheric research.

cards.headline: Medicaid work requirements finalized by Trump administration
cards.teaser: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services issued a final rule requiring most Medicaid recipients to work or volunteer.
cards.body:
The Trump administration issued a final rule requiring most Medicaid beneficiaries between ages 19 and 64 to document work or community service activities to maintain coverage. This represents a significant change to the Medicaid program's eligibility requirements.

Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, addressed the new requirements at a White House briefing Tuesday afternoon.

cards.headline: New Mexico lawmakers subpoena agencies in Epstein investigation
cards.teaser: A bipartisan committee investigating Jeffrey Epstein's New Mexico ranch issued its first round of subpoenas.
cards.body:
A special committee of New Mexico lawmakers announced Monday it will send subpoenas to 14 entities as part of its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein's Zorro Ranch near Santa Fe. The bipartisan New Mexico Truth Commission is targeting agencies that previously investigated Epstein's activities at the property.

The subpoenas represent the committee's first major step in examining Epstein's operations at the New Mexico property and how various government agencies responded to the situation.

cards.headline: Los Angeles mayor Bass faces primary challenge
cards.teaser: Incumbent Karen Bass is running for reelection against Nithya Raman and Spencer Pratt in the Los Angeles mayoral primary.
cards.body:
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass is seeking reelection in a primary race against two challengers. Nithya Raman and Spencer Pratt are competing against the incumbent in what observers describe as a tight contest.

Results from the primary election are being counted. The race will determine whether Bass can secure enough support to avoid a runoff or whether the contest will continue to a general election.
